utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the statement that was given to me by the father of this young man who got killed, he said to me that his son had come there to enroll in university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still not an answer to my question, because the question was whether you know personally whether classes were held. Do you know? Then please tell us. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not know whether classes were being held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the other question put to you by Mr. Lukic was: Do you have any knowledge of soldiers being stationed in that Faculty of Political Science building around that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 31, you say that the second shell hit the then JNA street as it was known then, and today it is known as the street of Branilaca Grada Sarajeva in front of the building of the Stari Grad municipality. Do you know what kind of military installations or units were in that building?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: That's the building of the Stari Grad municipality where clerks of that municipality work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there armed policemen standing in front of that building?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, is it correct that the centre for reconnaissance and reporting was in that building?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Only if from the -- before the war that was still there, that is to say that the municipality is the place from which reporting comes on fires and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You say the third shell landed on Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street, which was called Marsala Tita Street at the time. Can you tell us the exact date when the three shells you describe landed there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: The record of the on-site investigation contains the exact date. There were too many dates for me to remember them all. I can't tell you really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although this is not in the indictment, let us tie in the incident of February 1994, that is to say Markale I, and Markale II of August 1995. As you sit here today, would you say that both these shells were fired from Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Let me say this: The report produced by experts is the only true finding in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already heard you say that you never checked if the shells had come from the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will nevertheless ask you this: Did you double-check the statements that one of these shells was actually thrown by hand out of one of the buildings facing Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Judging by the reports which state that this was a 120-millimetre shell which exploded at Markale, it is hard to conceive of the possibility that somebody would be throwing such a shell out of an enclosed space and that such a shell would then explode in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we started by tying Markale I with Markale II. Then you asked a question about both the incidents, and slowly we move to one or still both of the incidents? That's unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman can't connect any rumour like this to any of these explosions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the witness said judging by the report which stated this was a 120-millimetre, then he apparently has one incident on his mind. Did you refer to Markale I in your answer where you said that the report stated that it was a 120-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these stories that the shell was a 120-millimetre shell had to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was did you refer to Markale I or to any other incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Markale I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be your question is broader than the witness understands it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: Did you investigate the matter in relation to the incident known as Markale II?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: No. We didn't have the power to investigate into this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you served your military service handling mortars. Can we agree that the mortar shell does not contain bomblets or pellets?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. When I served the army in the 1980s, I did not come across any shells that would contain within them pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know or did you come across information to the effect that there were individuals who were wounded during the Markale II incident as a result of being hit by -- by pellets, that they had thus shaped injuries?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I only took the statement of one of the persons wounded in Markale II, and the statement had to do with shrapnel rather than pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also asked about whether you participated in the investigations taking place at the scene of Markale II and you said no, so you cannot really tell us what direction was from which the shell that exploded at Markale II had come from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you cannot tell you [as interpreted] what type of projectile exploded at the location; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time or do you know today that on the 28th of August, 1995, UNPROFOR representatives did not detect any sort of artillery activity from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information to the effect that UNPROFOR detected the fire that had come from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the extent that you can tell us about the incident of Markale II, you said that there was a ban in force against civilians moving about the town. Is it true that in your subsequent testimonies you said that you didn't know who issued the ban, only to say at a later stage that you weren't really sure whether the ban was in force at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was a ban on movement in Sarajevo. I said that there was -- well, not an order. It was stated that there was to be no assembling or lingering in the locations where food provisions could be obtained and that people should spend there as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You yourself said that the streets and the whole area of Markale was suitable for movement because it was protected. This is my question: Is it true that there could be no clear line of sight of that area from any of the VRS positions?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: That area cannot be seen from any vantage point within the town itself either. One could only see the eastward direction. The positions at Borje could have a view because it coincided with the direction itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Borje within the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: It is yet another elevation on the edge of Sarajevo to the east in the direction of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the surroundings of Markale there were the reserve police units stationed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: The Stari Grad public security station, as was the case before and after the war, had policemen deployed into the individual local communes. This did not apply to reserve police forces only but also to the active force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will just view a short video-clip now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you want the Chamber to seriously consider the matters you are raising, then it would certainly help us to know where the Stari Grad public security station was exactly, in what street, what location, so we are able to establish what the distance was to where the shells fell, but if you just are talking about streets -- or is it on the video? I hope too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With the help of the witness, we can maybe learn more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps. Let's first watch the video. Is there any sound on the video, Mr. Lukic? I mean sounds -- any words spoken, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are not going to rely on sound or anything said, just the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we only play it only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djozo, do you know that in this passage that we saw the armed person coming out of twice was the headquarters of the quartermaster service of the 1st Corps in the immediate vicinity of Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that. What I do know is that there was a bakery there. There was also a general store located there which wasn't open at the time. And even if it was, there were very few goods to be obtained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the Stari Grad police station and Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Five hundred metres, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Stari Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: If there was a staff, then it could only have been housed in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know where it was located?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know that there was the quartermaster's storage of the 1st Corps headquartered in this passage that we saw the man in the footage come out of?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, I wasn't aware of the fact that they even had had a quartermaster's storage place. All I know is that all those wounded and killed were transported to the state hospital and the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you should have stated that you stopped at video at 17 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was the footage from 3:28 to -- at least that was indicated, 3:28 to 3:41.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can finish the video again. We can play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could we ask the witness -- apparently, Mr. Lukic, you are focusing on the person at the extreme left of the video where there seems to be kind of a yellow -- yellow stripe, a person --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Behind that yellow stripe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Behind that yellow stripe a person coming out and going back soon after that. Is that -- not really appearing in full. Is that what you're focusing on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the witness also to know that that is specifically what has the attention of Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have a more general question now for you. Is it true that you never saw a single report by ballistics officers from the centre? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: That's right. According to the rules of service, the ballistics reports produced in the CSB are sent to the investigating judge in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let us be specific as well. You did not see such reports in respect of Ms. Dervisa Selmanovic or in respect of Ibro Podrug. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: All the various sections produced their respective reports and sent them to the investigating judge in charge. By the same token, I was not able to see these reports ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, you never received or reviewed a single report compiled by doctors that had to do with injuries sustained from shells, bullets, and grenades during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: All medical findings, if any policeman went to the hospital and took such findings, in this specific case I'm speaking about Selmanovic, if this kind of report was received, again it was sent to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again I will have to conclude that you never saw any such report.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I did see a report on the wounding of Mrs. Selmanovic, whatever her first name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dervisa.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: That was submitted to the CSB and the investigative judge. Those were the appropriate institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D445. This is the transcript from the Perisic trial of the 18th of March. 4549 is the page we need. It's page 36 in e-court. I have the wrong number in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the page of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but obviously I jotted down the wrong number of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have an e-court number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do have it in e-court. I just have to find it. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's about medical findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now looking at e-court page 37, which is transcript page in that case 4550.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English so that you can get the proper interpretation of that. This is what they asked you, line 11: [In English] "Q. Did you ask the doctor to provide you with a report about the nature of her wounds? "A. No. At the time, nobody did that. We did not ask for medical findings." [Interpretation] Is it correct, therefore, that you did not ask for medical reports from doctors at the time, that no one did that, and that you did not request medical reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: In some cases when there was major shelling and therefore people were wounded and killed, at that moment it was impossible to get such findings. These findings were issued to injured persons, and then police officials would interview these persons and take the findings involved and submit them to the persons in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shall have to -- I shall have to take you back briefly to this. Obviously, this is a reference to Mrs. Selmanovic, because it says "report on her wounds, the nature of her words." So it is in the singular, and the gender is feminine. So what is the correct out of the two, that you requested a report and received it or that you did not request it and did not receive it?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: The doctor who admitted Mrs. Selmanovic gave her these findings, so it was only several months later that we managed to find the lady, and it was only then that we got these findings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now there's a new line of questioning that opens up. Could you conclude whether -- or, rather, could you conclude on the basis of that what kind of weapon wounded Mrs. Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't have her statement here, but when we found her in her apartment, the lady said that she had been wounded by a firearm that fired from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asim Zulic, does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I don't know who Asim Zulic is. The last name is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kemal Djozo, do you know who that is, a military man? Is he a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: A relative who worked in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the course of the war, was Mr. Kemal Djozo involved in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I met Kemal while he was still at the military academy in Zadar, and I saw him sometime in 2009 in Ohrid. In a conversation with him, I heard him say that he spent the entire war in Macedonia and that together with Mladic he was in the barracks there, that he stayed on in the barracks and continued his education and that he's a professor somewhere at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Let us now move on to those improvised bombs made of bottles. You were asked about that, and you said that you personally did not carry out an investigation about that because you were not qualified to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Just tell me what kind of bombs we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Improvised ones made of bottles.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Made of bottles. As for these bottles, I heard about them during the war, but towards the end of the war, I actually did see them underneath Osmica, above the neighbourhood of Sirokaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D444 on our screens now, please. I have page 72. We need page 9624, lines 5 through 11. In answer to the question which says. "Q. You saw an unexploded gas cylinder with wheels and another unexploited oil barrel that had wheels attached to it. Did this perhaps not call for a detailed investigation and a photo documentation, and was such an investigation ever carried out?" You said in line 9: "A. No, I never did such an investigation, because I'm not qualified for that." Is it therefore true that you did not investigate what this was about?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I did not investigate that, but my superiors were informed about this. An Official Note was compiled. Probably some of the ballistics people were made aware of this, and probably it was a ballistics person that carried out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need page 79 of this same document in e-court, otherwise, it is page 9631 from the Karadzic trial. The date is the 10th of December, 2010, and the lines are from 22 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When speaking about that you said: [In English] "The photographs were made by the person who signed the photographs, and he probably stated that there were explosives inside. He's the only one who can say that this was so." [Interpretation] My question now: Is it correct that you personally cannot confirm that these barrels or whatever were filled with explosive?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see it's break time, Your Honour, and I will have only a few questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break first and be -- after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following: The Chamber has considered the objections raised against the admission of Exhibit P514 that was marked for identification on Thursday, the 15th of November, during the testimony of Francis Roy Thomas and has decided to admit it into evidence, and the Chamber informs the parties that it is still to decide on the admission of the two other exhibits marked for identification in respect to that same witness, that is, P503 and P512. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are near the end, Mr. Djozo, but I do have a couple of questions left for you. As a policeman and later as an inspector, in how many investigations did you take part which involved Serbian civilians killed in the area covered by your police station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: I can't remember. We didn't keep a record based on whether a person was a Serb or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in investigations about the killings of Serbian civilians in Kazani, which is an area that comes under your police station, does it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kazani only once after the war, maybe in 1997 or 1998, when I think it was investigators from Belgrade arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate the prisons that kept Serbian individuals in the area under your purview? And I mean private prisons.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the municipality of Stari Grad and more generally in Sarajevo, there were no private prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Those are all the questions I had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could either the witness or you, Mr. Lukic, assist me in where to find approximately Kazani is, what area approximately. We don't need maps, but if you tell me approximately where to find it, then ... Witness, if you -- if you can tell me, Kazani is found where approximately? Just give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kazani is situated on the slopes of Trebevic, above the neighbourhood of Mahmutovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mahmutovac is where in relation to, for example, Sirokaca? More to the west, more to the east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm just trying to find it. Is it close to Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say that it was close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have an idea of where it is. Mr. Lukic, if you want to consult with Mr. Mladic, I'll give an opportunity at the end of the witness's testimony if otherwise the witness would be gone and you would have missed some instructions, but -- so -- but you know the rule is we would then take a very short break for that at the end of the testimony, but the rule is no consultations in the courtroom. No further questions at this moment. Mr. Weber, any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have no questions either, Mr. Djozo, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I'd like to deliver an oral decision; that is, an oral decision on admission of associated exhibits tendered with Witness Tucker. The Chamber has examined the submissions by the parties with regard to the associated exhibits tendered with witness Pyers Tucker and hereby renders its decision on their admissibility. The Chamber grants the Prosecution's request for leave to reply filed on the 19th of October of this year. At the outset, the Chamber reiterates that its guidance in relation to the tendering of evidence does not bar the admission of any evidence but aims at the clearest possible presentation thereof. The Chamber recalls that the case law with regard to the admission of associated exhibits pursuant to Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater establishes that documents can be admitted if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. This means that the witness needs to have discussed the exhibits in his testimony and that without them the transcript or the witness's written statement would be incomprehensible or of lesser probative value. The Chamber elaborated further on its approach to associated exhibits in the additional clarification and amendment of its guidance on the 9th of July, 2012, to be found on transcript pages 530 and 531. Therefore, in cases in which the Prosecution argued that the tendered exhibits provides information beyond what the witness stated, it does not qualify in that respect as an exhibit which is an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement or the evidence of the witness. The Chamber notes that the relevance and probative value of such exhibits may be considered in a different context. Further, in cases in which the tendered exhibits mainly corroborates the evidence of the witness, there may not be a need to tender it, though such tendering may become necessary upon a challenge of the witness's evidence in that respect if the exhibit has the potential to counter that challenge. The Chamber has reviewed the witness statement against the background of this test for admission of associated exhibits and the Chamber's guidance. The Chamber notes that often lengthy parts of associated exhibits were quoted in the witness statement, admitted as Exhibit P317, which leads the Chamber to the conclusion that these were the relevant sections that the Prosecution wanted to draw the Chamber's attention to. Under these circumstances, there is no need to tender the exhibits referred to in the witness statement. While the Chamber considers that 11 out of the 35 tendered associated exhibits are needed to properly understand the witness statement of Pyers Tucker, it finds with regard to the remaining 24 documents tendered as associated exhibits, that the witness statement was perfectly comprehensible on its own. Lastly, the Chamber notes the Defence's submissions of not having enough time to adequately address such large numbers of associated exhibits and challenge them as part of the cross-examination. In this regard, the Chamber points out that the Defence may always ask for additional time, especially if the tendered associated exhibits are voluminous. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber admits only the following 11 documents into evidence as associated exhibits to the evidence of witness Tucker: 65 ter number 3396, 3406, 9328, 9564, 11245, 11249, 11254, 11255, 13710, 15906, 19039A. With regard to the remaining associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution, the Chamber denies admission into evidence. The Registrar is invited to assign exhibit numbers, and since we have sufficient time at this moment, it could be done immediately.
